claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases under conventional rapid or slower cooling.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
Ultra-rapid melt-spinning at cooling rates on the order of 10^6 K/s will maximize the alloy's initial amorphous content.
A cooling rate greater than 10^6 K/s is sufficiently fast to suppress initial nucleation in this alloy.
The proposed post-quench annealing temperature is approximately 0.8–0.9 Tg.
The proposed sub-Tg hold should last from seconds to a few minutes.
Sub-Tg annealing will relieve residual internal stresses in the amorphous matrix.
Sub-Tg annealing will reduce free volume in the amorphous matrix.
Reduced stress and free volume will produce a more relaxed, thermally stable glass structure.
The relaxed glass structure will be less prone to heterogeneous nucleation of primary crystalline phases.
Controlled atomic rearrangements during the sub-Tg hold will lower the amorphous structure's internal energy.
Structural relaxation during the hold will quench potential crystallization nucleation sites.
The proposed relaxation will raise the activation barrier for crystallization during subsequent reheating.
Sub-Tg annealing will shift the DSC crystallization onset to a higher temperature relative to an identically quenched, unannealed sample.
Sub-Tg annealing will diminish the crystallization-exotherm intensity during DSC reheating.
Sub-Tg annealing will yield a higher retained amorphous fraction than the as-quenched baseline.
A hold that is too long or too hot may cause unwanted nucleation.
Sub-Tg annealing has enhanced thermal stability in other metallic-glass systems.

contradictions.description: The anneal is described both as being just below the crystallization onset and as 0.8–0.9 Tg. A temperature below Tg is generally not equivalent to a temperature just below the crystallization onset, so the operative thermal boundary is internally ambiguous.
